title: Phase 1 — Java Language Foundations
summary: The language and the JVM underneath it: types and references, the equals/hashCode contract that quietly breaks collections, exceptions, and the modern features that removed most of Java's old verbosity.
outcomes: Read Java and predict what it does, including reference behaviour
Implement equals and hashCode correctly, and know what breaks without them
Choose between checked and unchecked exceptions with a reason
Use records, var, switch expressions and text blocks instead of legacy boilerplate
Explain what the JVM does between your source and the running program

modules.title: The Language and the JVM
modules.summary: How Java runs, and the reference semantics behind most beginner confusion.

lessons.title: From Source to JVM: What Actually Runs
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Compiled twice

`javac` turns your `.java` files into bytecode in `.class` files. The JVM then executes that bytecode, compiling the hot paths to machine code as it runs.

This two-stage arrangement is why the same jar runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and why a long-running Java service gets faster in the first minutes of its life — the just-in-time compiler is still optimising what turns out to be hot.

## Everything lives in a class, mostly

Historically every line of Java had to sit inside a class. Modern Java has relaxed this for simple programs, but real projects still organise code into packages and classes, and you should expect to see the traditional form everywhere.

## Primitives and objects are different things

`int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean` and `char` are primitives. They hold their value directly and cannot be null.

Everything else is an object, accessed through a reference. `Integer` is the object wrapper around `int`, and it *can* be null.

## Autoboxing is convenient and occasionally sharp

Java converts between `int` and `Integer` automatically. That is usually invisible and occasionally painful: unboxing a null `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException` at a line that looks like simple arithmetic.

It also means `==` on two `Integer` objects compares references, not values. For anything outside a small cached range, two equal `Integer`s can be `!=`. Use `.equals()` for object comparison and primitives where you can.

## Garbage collection, briefly

You do not free memory; the JVM reclaims objects nothing references. You mostly ignore this, but it explains two things: why holding a reference in a long-lived collection is how Java leaks memory, and why pauses occasionally appear in latency graphs.
keyTakeaways: Source compiles to bytecode, which the JVM runs and progressively optimises
Primitives hold values and cannot be null; everything else is a reference
Autoboxing can throw a NullPointerException on a line that looks like arithmetic
`==` compares references for objects — use `.equals()` for value comparison
Memory leaks in Java are references held too long, usually in a long-lived collection

questions.prompt: Why can `Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b` be false?
questions.explanation: `==` on objects compares references. Two separately created Integer objects outside the small cached range are distinct, so reference comparison fails despite equal values.

options.text: `==` compares references, and these are two distinct objects
Integer values above 999 lose precision
`==` is not defined for Integer
The values are stored as doubles internally

questions.prompt: What is the risk of autoboxing?
questions.explanation: Unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException at a line containing only what looks like arithmetic, which makes it hard to spot.

options.text: Unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException on an innocuous-looking line
It silently truncates large values
It prevents the use of generics
It disables garbage collection for that object

lessons.title: equals, hashCode and Why Collections Break Without Them
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The contract

Two methods, inherited by every object, with a contract between them:

- If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` **must** be true.
- Equal hash codes do not imply equality — collisions are allowed.

Break the first rule and hash-based collections stop working, silently.

## Why it breaks silently

A `HashMap` finds a key by computing its hash code, going to that bucket, and comparing with `equals`. If you override `equals` but not `hashCode`, two equal objects get different hash codes, land in different buckets, and the map never finds the one you stored.

You put a value in with a key and get `null` back with an equal key. No exception, no warning — just a wrong answer. The same applies to `HashSet`, which will happily hold duplicates.

## Default behaviour is identity

Inherited `equals` compares references and inherited `hashCode` is derived from identity. For a value-like class — a customer id, a money amount, a coordinate — that is almost never what you want.

## Records do it for you

A `record` generates `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from its components. For data carriers, that removes the entire problem and is the right default in modern Java.

Write them by hand only when you need something the record cannot express, such as equality on a subset of fields.

## If you write them by hand, use the helpers

`Objects.equals` handles nulls and `Objects.hash` combines fields. There is no reason to hand-roll either.

## Mutable keys are a trap

If you put an object in a `HashSet` and then change a field that `hashCode` uses, its hash changes but its bucket does not. The object is now in the wrong place and the set cannot find it — including when you ask whether it contains it. Keys should be effectively immutable.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TB A["map.get(key)"] --> B["hashCode() -> bucket"] B --> C{Bucket found?} C -->|"no: hashCode differs"| D["returns null
SILENTLY WRONG"] C -->|yes| E["equals() within bucket"] E --> F[Value returned]
keyTakeaways: Equal objects must have equal hash codes; the reverse is not required
Overriding equals without hashCode makes HashMap and HashSet silently fail
Default equality is identity, which is wrong for value-like classes
Records generate equals, hashCode and toString — the right default for data
Never mutate a field used by hashCode while the object is a key in a hash collection

questions.prompt: You override `equals` but not `hashCode` and use the class as a HashMap key. What happens?
questions.explanation: Equal objects produce different hash codes, so they land in different buckets. The lookup never reaches the equals comparison and returns null.

options.text: Lookups return null for keys that are equal, with no error
The map throws an IllegalStateException
The map falls back to equals and works correctly but slowly
The compiler refuses to build

questions.prompt: Why must a field used by `hashCode` not be mutated while the object is a key in a HashSet?
questions.explanation: The object stays in the bucket chosen by its original hash. After mutation the set looks in a different bucket and cannot find it.

options.text: The object stays in its original bucket and becomes unfindable
The set automatically rehashes and the operation is slow
It throws a ConcurrentModificationException
Nothing — HashSet recomputes hashes on every access

modules.title: Collections, Generics and Streams
modules.summary: The standard library you will use every day, and the type safety behind it.

lessons.title: Collections and Generics
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Program to the interface

Declare variables as `List`, `Map` or `Set`, and choose the implementation at construction:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

Callers depend only on the interface, so you can change `ArrayList` to `LinkedList` without touching them.

## Choosing an implementation

- **`ArrayList`** — the default. Fast indexed access, fast iteration.
- **`LinkedList`** — rarely the right answer. Its theoretical insert advantage is usually lost to poor cache behaviour.
- **`HashMap`** — the default map. No ordering guarantee.
- **`LinkedHashMap`** — preserves insertion order, which matters more often than people expect.
- **`TreeMap`** — sorted by key, at a cost.
- **`HashSet`** — membership and uniqueness.

## Generics are compile-time only

`List<String>` prevents you inserting an `Integer` at compile time. At runtime the type parameter is erased and it is just a `List`.

This *erasure* explains several limitations: you cannot write `new T[]`, you cannot test `instanceof List<String>`, and you cannot overload two methods that differ only by type parameter.

## Immutable collections for constants

`List.of(...)` and `Map.of(...)` create immutable collections. Use them for anything that should not change — a caller cannot accidentally modify your constant, and the intent is visible.

Note they reject nulls, which is usually a feature.

## Watch for accidental exposure

Returning your internal `ArrayList` lets callers modify your object's state directly. Return `List.copyOf(internal)` or `Collections.unmodifiableList(internal)` when the caller should only read.
keyTakeaways: Declare the interface, construct the implementation
ArrayList and HashMap are the defaults; LinkedHashMap when order matters
Generics are erased at runtime, which explains several odd limitations
`List.of` and `Map.of` create immutable collections and reject nulls
Never return your internal mutable collection directly

questions.prompt: What does type erasure mean for generics in Java?
questions.explanation: Type parameters exist for the compiler and are removed from the runtime representation, which is why `new T[]` and `instanceof List<String>` are not possible.

options.text: Type parameters are checked at compile time and removed at runtime
Generic types are checked at runtime via reflection
Generics are converted to Object with automatic casts that can fail silently
Each type parameter generates a separate compiled class

questions.prompt: Why return `List.copyOf(internal)` rather than the internal list itself?
questions.explanation: Handing out the internal list lets any caller mutate the object's state directly, bypassing every rule the class enforces.

options.text: It prevents callers mutating the object's internal state
It is faster than returning the reference
The internal list cannot be serialised
It converts the list to an array internally

lessons.title: Streams, Lambdas and Optional
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Streams express the what

A stream pipeline has a source, zero or more intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`), and one terminal operation (`collect`, `count`, `findFirst`) that makes it run.

Nothing happens until the terminal operation. Intermediate operations only build the pipeline.

## Lambdas and method references

`c -> c.getRegion()` is a lambda. `Customer::getRegion` is a method reference doing the same thing more briefly. Use the method reference when it reads clearly.

## Collectors do the grouping

`Collectors.groupingBy` is the one to know. It turns a flat stream into a map, and combined with a downstream collector it produces exactly the aggregate you want in one expression.

## Optional is a return type, not a field

`Optional<T>` exists so a method can say "there may be no result" in its signature instead of returning null and hoping.

Use it as a return type. Do not use it for fields or method parameters — it adds allocation and awkwardness without adding clarity.

And never call `.get()` without checking. `orElse`, `orElseThrow` and `map` are the point; `.get()` reintroduces exactly the failure Optional was meant to remove.

## Do not reach for parallel streams

`parallelStream()` looks like free speed and rarely is. It uses a shared thread pool, helps only with large CPU-bound work, and behaves badly with I/O. Measure before using it, and assume the answer is no.

## Keep pipelines readable

A pipeline nobody can read is worse than the loop it replaced. If it exceeds a handful of operations, extract a named method for part of it.
keyTakeaways: A stream does nothing until its terminal operation runs
Method references are shorter than lambdas where they read clearly
`Collectors.groupingBy` with a downstream collector produces aggregates in one expression
Optional is for return types; `.get()` without checking defeats its purpose
Parallel streams are rarely a win — measure, and expect the answer to be no

questions.prompt: When does a stream pipeline actually execute?
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations are lazy and only build the pipeline. The terminal operation drives execution.

options.text: When the terminal operation runs
As each intermediate operation is written
When the stream is created from the source
At compile time

questions.prompt: What is the recommended use of `Optional`?
questions.explanation: Optional communicates possible absence in a return signature. As a field or parameter it adds allocation and awkwardness without clarity, and `.get()` defeats it entirely.

options.text: As a method return type, consumed with map, orElse or orElseThrow
As a field type to avoid null fields
As a method parameter to make arguments optional
As a replacement for exceptions in all error cases

modules.title: Errors and Modern Java
modules.summary: Exception design, and the features that removed Java's reputation for verbosity.

lessons.title: Checked and Unchecked Exceptions
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Java's unusual choice

Java has two kinds. **Checked** exceptions (extending `Exception`) must be declared or caught — the compiler enforces it. **Unchecked** exceptions (extending `RuntimeException`) need neither.

No other mainstream language does this, and opinion on whether it was a good idea remains divided. What matters is knowing how to use each.

## When each is appropriate

Use a **checked** exception when the caller can plausibly recover: a file that might not exist, a network call that might time out. The compiler forces them to think about it.

Use an **unchecked** exception for programming errors and unrecoverable conditions: a null argument that should never be null, an invalid state, a configuration value that is missing at startup.

## Never swallow one

```java
try { risky(); } catch (Exception e) { }
```

This is the worst construct in Java. A failure becomes a silently wrong result and the log says nothing. If you genuinely cannot handle it, do not catch it.

## Do not declare `throws Exception`

It tells the caller nothing and forces them into the same broad catch. Declare the specific exceptions you actually throw.

## Wrap, preserving the cause

When crossing a layer boundary, wrap a low-level exception in a domain one — and always pass the original as the cause. Losing the cause means losing the stack trace that says what really happened.

## try-with-resources for anything closeable

It closes resources even when an exception is thrown, and unlike a `finally` block it cannot be got wrong. Use it for every stream, connection and reader.
keyTakeaways: Checked exceptions must be declared or caught; unchecked ones need neither
Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors
An empty catch block turns a failure into a silently wrong result
Declare specific exceptions, never `throws Exception`
Wrap across layers but always pass the cause; use try-with-resources for closeables

questions.prompt: When is a checked exception the appropriate choice?
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions force the caller to consider a condition they can plausibly recover from. Programming errors should be unchecked.

options.text: When the caller can plausibly recover, such as a missing file or a timeout
For any error that must not be ignored, including programming bugs
Whenever the method performs I/O of any kind
For errors originating in third-party libraries

questions.prompt: Why pass the original exception as the cause when wrapping?
questions.explanation: The cause carries the original stack trace. Dropping it leaves you with a domain exception and no information about what actually failed.

options.text: It preserves the original stack trace, without which the failure is undiagnosable
It is required by the compiler
It converts the exception to unchecked
It allows the exception to be caught twice

lessons.title: Records, Sealed Types and Pattern Matching
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Java stopped being verbose

Much of Java's reputation came from features that are now obsolete. A data class that took forty lines takes one. Type checks that needed a cast on the next line no longer do.

If you learned Java before version 17 — or from older tutorials — a large amount of what you were taught is now the long way round.

## Records replace the data class

```java
record Customer(String id, String name, String region) { }
```

That gives you a constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. Records are immutable, which makes them safe to share and easy to reason about.

Add validation in a compact constructor when the record has rules.

## Sealed types close the set

`sealed interface` names exactly which types may implement it. Two things follow: nobody can add a case you did not anticipate, and the compiler knows the full set, so a `switch` over it can be checked for exhaustiveness.

That combination — a closed set of cases plus a switch the compiler verifies — is how you model "one of these outcomes" so that adding a new outcome produces a compile error everywhere it must be handled.

## Pattern matching removes the cast

`if (o instanceof Customer c)` tests and binds in one step. Switch patterns extend this to a full dispatch, and with records you can destructure the components directly in the pattern.

## Prefer immutability

Records are immutable by default and that is the right default. An immutable object cannot be corrupted by another thread, cannot change under a caller who is iterating, and can be shared freely.

Reach for mutability when you have a measured reason, not by habit.
keyTakeaways: A record generates constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString
Compact constructors let a record validate its own components
Sealed types close the set of implementations and enable exhaustive switches
Pattern matching tests and binds in one step, and can destructure records
Immutability by default: safe to share, cannot change under a caller

questions.prompt: What does a `sealed` interface combined with a switch give you?
questions.explanation: The compiler knows every permitted implementation, so it can verify the switch handles all of them. Adding a case then breaks the build where it must be handled.

options.text: Compile-time exhaustiveness checking, so a new case breaks the build where it must be handled
Faster dispatch at runtime
Automatic serialisation of all implementations
Prevention of null values

questions.prompt: Why does adding a `default` branch to a switch over a sealed type reduce safety?
questions.explanation: The default absorbs unhandled cases, so the compiler stops reporting them. A new subtype then silently falls into default instead of failing the build.

options.text: It disables exhaustiveness checking, so new cases fall through silently
It makes the switch slower
It is a compile error on sealed types
It prevents record destructuring in the other branches

modules.title: Spring and Dependency Injection
modules.summary: What the container does, and why your classes should not construct their own dependencies.

lessons.title: What Spring Actually Does at Startup
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The container builds your object graph

At startup Spring scans for annotated classes, works out what each one needs from its constructor, and instantiates them in dependency order. Those objects are *beans*, and Spring hands them to whatever asks.

The problem being solved is the same as in any language: a class that constructs its own dependencies cannot be tested, cannot be reconfigured, and has decided something it had no business deciding.

## Constructor injection, always

Declare dependencies as constructor parameters and mark the fields `final`. Spring supplies them.

Avoid field injection with `@Autowired` on a field. It hides the dependencies from anyone reading the constructor, prevents `final`, and makes the class impossible to instantiate in a plain unit test without reflection.

Constructor injection makes an over-dependent class visibly uncomfortable — six parameters is a design signal you want to see.

## The stereotype annotations

`@Component` is the general case. `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@Controller` are the same thing with intent attached, and a little extra behaviour in the case of `@Repository`, which translates persistence exceptions.

Use the specific one; it documents the layer.

## Auto-configuration

Spring Boot inspects your classpath and configures what it finds. A JDBC driver present means a `DataSource` is configured from your properties. This is why a Boot application needs so little setup — and why understanding it matters when it configures something you did not want.

`--debug` prints the auto-configuration report, which is the fastest way to answer "why is this bean here?"

## Beans are singletons by default

One instance, shared by everything. That makes shared mutable state in a bean a concurrency bug affecting every request at once. Keep beans stateless.
keyTakeaways: Spring builds the object graph from constructor parameters at startup
Use constructor injection with final fields; field injection hides dependencies
Many constructor parameters is a visible design signal worth keeping
Auto-configuration reacts to the classpath; `--debug` explains what it chose
Beans are singletons — mutable state in one is a concurrency bug for every request

questions.prompt: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies visible and final, allows plain instantiation in tests, and makes an over-dependent class visibly uncomfortable.

options.text: Dependencies are visible and final, and the class can be instantiated in a test without reflection
It is faster at startup
Field injection is deprecated and will be removed
It allows circular dependencies to be resolved

questions.prompt: Why is mutable state in a Spring bean usually a bug?
questions.explanation: Beans default to singleton scope, so one instance serves every concurrent request and any mutable field becomes shared state.

options.text: Beans are singletons by default, so the state is shared across all concurrent requests
Spring forbids non-final fields in beans
It prevents the bean from being proxied
It causes the bean to be recreated on each request

lessons.title: Building REST Endpoints That Behave
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Controllers stay thin

A controller binds the request, calls a service and maps the result. Business rules in a controller cannot be tested without the web layer and cannot be reused.

## Never expose your JPA entities

An entity carries persistence concerns, lazy-loading proxies and fields the caller should not see. Serialising one directly couples your public API to your database schema, and triggers lazy-loading exceptions outside a transaction.

Define request and response records. The mapping is a few lines and it buys you a stable contract.

## Validate declaratively

Annotate the request record with `@NotBlank`, `@Positive`, `@Size` and mark the parameter `@Valid`. A violation produces a 400 before your method runs.

Add a handler so the body names the offending fields — the default is not especially helpful to a client developer.

## Status codes carry meaning

- **201** with a `Location` header when you create something.
- **204** for a successful delete.
- **404** when the resource does not exist.
- **409** when the request is valid but conflicts with current state — a movement that would make stock negative.
- **400** when the request itself is wrong.

The 400-versus-409 distinction matters to callers: a 409 may succeed later, a 400 will not.

## Handle exceptions in one place

`@RestControllerAdvice` maps domain exceptions to responses centrally, so every controller returns the same error shape and no controller repeats the mapping.

## Do not leak internals

Never return a stack trace. Log it with a request id and return the id.
keyTakeaways: Controllers bind, delegate and map — rules belong in the service
Never serialise JPA entities; define request and response records
Validate with annotations plus `@Valid`, and return field-level errors
409 for a state conflict, 400 for a malformed request — only one is retryable
Map exceptions centrally with `@RestControllerAdvice`; never return stack traces

questions.prompt: Why should JPA entities not be returned directly from a controller?
questions.explanation: Entities carry lazy proxies and persistence concerns, and returning them couples the public API to the database schema so a migration silently changes the contract.

options.text: They couple the API to the database schema and can trigger lazy-loading failures
They cannot be converted to JSON
They are always slower to serialise
Spring forbids it at compile time

questions.prompt: A movement request is well-formed but would make stock negative. Which status code?
questions.explanation: The request is valid; the current state conflicts. That is 409, and it may succeed later once stock arrives.

options.text: 409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
422 Unprocessable Entity, which is the only correct option
500 Internal Server Error

modules.title: Configuration and Profiles
modules.summary: Running one build in several environments without editing it.

lessons.title: Properties, Profiles and Keeping Secrets Out
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Layered configuration

`application.yml` holds defaults. `application-{profile}.yml` overrides per environment. Environment variables override both, and command-line arguments override everything.

One artifact, three environments, no recompilation.

## Profiles

Activate with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`. Beans can be annotated `@Profile("dev")` so development-only components never load in production.

Resist letting profiles multiply. Two or three is manageable; eight interacting profiles is a configuration nobody can reason about.

## Type-safe configuration

`@ConfigurationProperties` binds a section to a record and validates it. Better than scattering `@Value("${...}")` strings: the names are checked at compile time, and a missing required value fails at startup with a clear message rather than injecting null.

Startup validation is the point. A misconfigured deployment should refuse to start, not fail at 2 a.m. on the first request that touches the missing value.

## Secrets never go in the repository

Passwords, API keys and certificates stay out of `application.yml` — the file is in Git, and Git keeps history forever. A committed key is leaked even after you delete it; it must be rotated.

Use environment variables locally and a secret manager in production. The `${VAR}` placeholder syntax reads them.

## Actuator, but not all of it

Spring Boot Actuator exposes health, metrics and environment endpoints. Health and metrics are genuinely useful. Expose only those — `/actuator/env` will happily print your configuration to anyone who can reach it.
lessons.codeExample:
# application.yml — defaults only, no secrets
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false        # default true; leaves a transaction open for the
                               # whole request and hides lazy-loading mistakes

inventory:
  low-stock-threshold: 10
  allow-negative: false

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics,info    # NOT "*" — /actuator/env prints config

---
# application-prod.yml — overrides for production
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}              # from the environment, never from this file
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate        # NEVER update or create-drop in production;
                                # validate fails fast if migrations did not run

inventory:
  low-stock-threshold: 25
keyTakeaways: Configuration layers: yml, profile yml, environment variables, command line
Profiles switch environments and can exclude beans; keep the number small
`@ConfigurationProperties` gives checked names and startup validation
Never commit a secret — Git history means it is leaked, not removed
Expose only the actuator endpoints you need; `/actuator/env` leaks configuration

questions.prompt: Why prefer `@ConfigurationProperties` over scattered `@Value` annotations?
questions.explanation: Binding to a type gives compile-checked names and lets validation run at startup, so a misconfigured deployment fails immediately rather than at 2 a.m.

options.text: Names are compile-checked and validation can fail the application at startup
`@Value` does not support environment variables
It is required for profiles to work
It reduces memory usage

questions.prompt: Why set `ddl-auto: validate` rather than `update` in production?
questions.explanation: `update` lets Hibernate alter the live schema by inference. `validate` fails fast when the schema does not match, which catches a migration that did not run.

options.text: It fails fast when the schema does not match, instead of letting Hibernate alter it by inference
`update` is not supported in production profiles
`validate` creates the schema if missing
It makes startup faster

lessons.title: Layering a Spring Application
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Three layers, one direction

**Controller** handles HTTP. **Service** holds business rules and transaction boundaries. **Repository** talks to the database.

Dependencies point one way: controller to service to repository. A repository that calls a service, or a service that knows about `HttpServletRequest`, has broken the arrangement and you will feel it when you try to test either.

## The service layer owns the rules

"Stock cannot go negative" belongs in the service, not the controller and not the database alone. Put it in the controller and it is bypassed by any other caller; put it only in the database and the error you surface is a constraint violation nobody can read.

Enforce in the service *and* constrain in the database. The service gives a good message; the constraint guarantees correctness under a race.

## Transactions belong at the service boundary

`@Transactional` on a service method makes the whole operation atomic. On a repository method it is too narrow — a service doing two repository calls gets two transactions and can leave half a change committed.

Two things to know: `@Transactional` works through a proxy, so calling one transactional method from another method *of the same class* bypasses it entirely. And a checked exception does not trigger rollback by default, which surprises people.

## Keep entities inside

Entities belong to the persistence layer. The controller sees request and response records; the service maps between them. That mapping is not overhead — it is the boundary that lets each side change independently.

## Test each layer for what it is

Service logic with fake repositories, fast. Repositories against a real database, because that is the only way to test your actual queries. Controllers through the real HTTP pipeline. Each layer tested where its risk lives.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TB A[Controller
HTTP, request/response records] --> B[Service
rules + @Transactional] B --> C[Repository
queries] C --> D[(Database
constraints back the rules)] B -.->|never| A C -.->|never| B
keyTakeaways: Controller, service, repository — dependencies point one way only
Business rules live in the service; enforce there and constrain in the database too
`@Transactional` belongs at the service boundary, not on repository methods
Self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional` because it works through a proxy
Entities stay in the persistence layer; map to records at the boundary

questions.prompt: Why does `@Transactional` belong on a service method rather than a repository method?
questions.explanation: A service operation often spans several repository calls. Transactions on each call means a failure can leave half the change committed.

options.text: A service operation spans several repository calls that must commit together
Repositories cannot participate in transactions
Service methods run faster inside transactions
Spring ignores the annotation on repositories

questions.prompt: Why does calling a `@Transactional` method from another method of the same class not start a transaction?
questions.explanation: The annotation is implemented by a proxy wrapping the bean. An internal call goes direct to the target object and never passes through the proxy.

options.text: The annotation works through a proxy, which an internal call bypasses
Nested transactions are not supported
The method must be public, and internal calls are treated as private
Spring caches the first call's transaction state

modules.title: Working with Data in Spring
modules.summary: Spring Data JPA: repositories, queries, and the traps that make them slow.

lessons.title: Entities, Repositories and Spring Data
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## JPA maps objects to tables

An `@Entity` class becomes a table, its fields become columns, and Hibernate translates between them. Spring Data adds repositories: declare an interface, get an implementation.

## Derived query methods

`findBySkuAndActiveTrue` is parsed from the method name and turned into a query. Convenient and readable — up to a point. When the name grows past about three conditions it becomes unreadable, and `@Query` with explicit JPQL is clearer.

## Know your identifiers

Use a generated id for the primary key, and place a unique constraint on the natural key. Hibernate needs a stable identifier, and a business key that might change makes a poor primary key.

## Avoid `ddl-auto: update` outside development

Letting Hibernate infer schema changes produces a database nobody designed, diverging between environments. Use Flyway or Liquibase: versioned, reviewable migrations committed with the code.

Then `ddl-auto: validate` in production confirms the schema matches and fails fast if a migration did not run.

## Fetch types matter

`@ManyToOne` defaults to eager, which quietly pulls related rows on every query. `@OneToMany` defaults to lazy, which throws if you touch it outside a transaction.

Set everything to lazy, and load explicitly where needed with a fetch join or an entity graph. Explicit is easier to reason about than a default you have to remember.

## Turn off open-in-view

Spring Boot defaults `spring.jpa.open-in-view` to true, keeping a transaction open for the whole request. It hides lazy-loading mistakes until production load makes them visible as exhausted connections.

Set it to false and fix what breaks. What breaks was already broken.

lessons.title: The N+1 Problem and Concurrency
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## N+1, the standard ORM defect

Load 100 stock items, then read `item.getWarehouse().getName()` on each. If warehouses were not fetched, Hibernate issues a query per item. One query became 101.

It is invisible with ten test rows and crippling with ten thousand production rows, which is why it so reliably reaches production.

## Detecting it

Enable SQL logging in development and watch the count during a normal operation. A page that issues 300 queries is not subtly slow — it is broken, and you can see it in seconds once you look.

Make looking a habit rather than a debugging step.

## Fixing it

A **fetch join** (`join fetch`) loads the association in the same query. An **entity graph** does the same declaratively. A **projection** to a record is often best: it selects only the columns you need and removes the possibility entirely, because there is nothing lazy left.

Note that `join fetch` on a collection plus pagination makes Hibernate paginate in memory — it warns about this, and the warning should be treated as an error.

## Concurrency: the lost update

Two requests read stock of 1, both decide there is enough, both write 0. One unit was sold twice. No exception, no log entry, just wrong data.

Two defences:

**Optimistic locking** — a `@Version` column. Each update checks the version has not changed; the loser gets an exception and can retry. Right when conflicts are rare.

**Pessimistic locking** — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. The second reader waits. Right when conflicts are common and retrying is awkward, as with stock movements.

## Constrain in the database too

Application logic cannot guarantee an invariant under concurrency by itself. A `CHECK (on_hand >= 0)` constraint is the backstop that makes the rule actually true, whatever the application does.

lessons.title: JUnit 5 and Testing the Service Layer
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Test behaviour, not implementation

A good test states a rule: "a movement that would make stock negative is rejected". It stays true when you refactor and fails when you break the rule.

A test asserting that `repository.save` was called exactly once is testing how the code is written, and breaks on every behaviour-preserving change. Enough of those and the team learns to ignore failures.

## Name the test as a sentence

`record_whenQuantityExceedsStock_throwsInsufficientStock`. The name is read in a CI failure list by someone who has not opened the file. It should be enough on its own.

## Arrange, act, assert

Three blocks, blank lines between. When there are two acts, there are two tests.

## Fakes over mocks where you can

A small in-memory repository tests behaviour: put stock in, take stock out, check the balance. Mockito verifying call sequences tests wiring.

Mockito is the right tool sometimes — particularly for something whose only observable effect is the call, such as sending an email. Reach for a fake first.

## The service layer needs no Spring

If dependencies come in through the constructor, a service test is plain JUnit with `new`. No context, no `@SpringBootTest`, milliseconds per test.

`@SpringBootTest` loads the whole application and belongs in a small number of integration tests, not across the suite. A suite that takes four minutes is a suite people stop running.

## Test the edges

Zero, one, the exact boundary, the failure. The comfortable middle case is the least likely to break.
keyTakeaways: Assert on behaviour, not on which methods were called

Prefer a small fake over call-verifying mocks; keep Mockito for call-is-the-effect cases

lessons.title: Integration Tests With the Real Stack
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What unit tests structurally cannot catch

Service tests replace the repository, so they never execute your JPA queries. Controller logic tested directly never exercises routing, serialisation or validation.

Every one of these passes a green unit suite and fails on the first real request: a query with a typo in a column name, a JSON field the client does not recognise, a bean that is not registered.

## Slices before the whole application

Spring offers focused test slices that load only part of the context:

- **`@DataJpaTest`** — the persistence layer with a real database. This is how you test that your queries actually work.
- **`@WebMvcTest`** — the web layer with services mocked. Tests routing, binding, validation and status codes.
- **`@SpringBootTest`** — everything. Use sparingly, for a few true end-to-end journeys.

Slices start in a fraction of the time and fail more specifically.

## Test against a real database

An in-memory H2 is not the database you deploy to. Its SQL dialect differs, and queries that pass against H2 fail against Postgres.

Testcontainers runs a real Postgres in Docker for the test. It is slower to start and it tests the thing you actually ship, which is the entire point of an integration test.

## Assert the contract

Status codes, response body shape, and the effect on stored state. Not which internal method ran — that is what unit tests are for.

## Cover the failure paths

The 404 and the 409 are the least manually exercised and the most depended on by clients.

## Keep the count low

A handful of integration tests plus thorough unit tests underneath is the right shape. Hundreds of slow tests produce a pipeline people route around.
keyTakeaways: Unit tests never execute your real queries, routing or serialisation
Use `@DataJpaTest` and `@WebMvcTest` slices before reaching for `@SpringBootTest`
Test persistence against a real database with Testcontainers, not H2
Assert status codes, response shape and stored state — not internal calls
Keep integration tests few; a slow pipeline gets routed around

modules.title: Concurrency
modules.summary: What actually goes wrong when two threads touch the same data.

lessons.title: Thread Safety Without Folklore
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Where concurrency reaches you

You may never start a thread, and you are still writing concurrent code. A Spring controller handles many requests simultaneously, and every singleton bean is shared between all of them.

Any mutable field on a bean is shared mutable state across concurrent requests. That is the whole problem, and the fix is almost always to have none.

## Stateless beans solve most of it

A service that holds nothing between calls cannot have a race. Keep state in parameters, local variables and the database.

This is not a compromise — it is the design that scales, and it is why the framework's defaults push you towards it.

## The lost update is the classic

Two threads read a value, both compute from it, both write back. One update vanishes. No exception, no log line, just a wrong number.

`count++` has exactly this shape: it reads, adds and writes, and another thread can interleave. It is not atomic despite looking like a single operation.

## Visibility is separate from atomicity

Without synchronisation, a write by one thread may not become visible to another for an unbounded time — the JVM and CPU are permitted to cache and reorder.

This produces the worst kind of bug: code that works on your laptop, works under light load, and fails under production load on different hardware.

## Reach for the right tool

- **Immutability** — no shared mutable state, no problem. Records help.
- **`AtomicInteger` / `AtomicLong`** — lock-free atomic counters.
- **`ConcurrentHashMap`** — a map safe for concurrent use. Note `computeIfAbsent` is atomic; a get-then-put is not.
- **`synchronized`** — correct and simple; just keep the block small.
- **Database locks** — the only thing that helps when the shared state is a row and there are several instances of your application.

## Do not invent your own

Double-checked locking, lazy singletons, custom lock-free structures — these are extremely easy to get subtly wrong, and the failures are rare and unreproducible. Use what the standard library provides.
keyTakeaways: Every singleton bean is shared across concurrent requests; mutable fields are shared state
Stateless services cannot race — keep state in parameters and the database
`count++` is read-modify-write and is not atomic
Visibility is a separate problem from atomicity, and produces load-dependent bugs
Use immutability, atomics, concurrent collections, synchronized or database locks — never your own

modules.title: Production Readiness
modules.summary: The health, logging and packaging an operations team needs before they will own it.

lessons.title: Health, Metrics and Packaging for Production
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Liveness and readiness are different questions

**Liveness**: is the process alive? If not, restart it.

**Readiness**: can it serve traffic? Database reachable, migrations applied, caches populated.

Conflating them means traffic routed to an instance that is running but cannot answer, and the resulting errors look exactly like an outage during every deployment.

Spring Boot Actuator exposes both, and a custom `HealthIndicator` lets you check whatever readiness actually means for your service.

## Expose the endpoints you need, and no more

`/actuator/health` and `/actuator/metrics` are useful. `/actuator/env` prints your configuration, and `/actuator/heapdump` hands over your memory.

Never set `include: "*"`. List them.

## Structured logging

Log with placeholders, not string concatenation: `log.info("Recorded movement {} for sku {}", id, sku)`. The values stay searchable fields, so "every event for this sku" is a query rather than a grep.

Add a correlation id to every request and put it in every log line via MDC. Then one id retrieves the whole story of a request across services.

## Log levels mean something

INFO for events worth seeing in production. WARN for recoverable problems a human should eventually look at. ERROR for failed operations. DEBUG for development.

Everything at INFO produces a volume nobody reads, which is equivalent to no logging.

## Package as one artifact

A Spring Boot jar is self-contained. Build once, promote the same artifact through environments, and inject configuration at each. An artifact rebuilt per environment is an artifact you have not tested.

## Layer the container image

Boot supports a layered jar so dependencies — which rarely change — sit in a lower Docker layer than your code. Rebuilds then push kilobytes rather than megabytes.
keyTakeaways: Liveness asks if the process is alive; readiness asks if it can serve
Expose only the actuator endpoints you need — never `include: "*"`

Reserve INFO for what is worth reading in production
